segments.say: Lesson 4. Tokens & Tokenization. How text becomes numbers, why "1 token about ¾ word", and why tokens decide cost, latency and limits.

A token is a small chunk of text (a word, part of a word, or punctuation) that an L L M reads and writes. Models see numbered tokens, never letters, and everything is priced and limited in tokens. Here is an analogy. L E G O bricks: a tokenizer has a fixed box of brick shapes. Common words are a single brick; rare words are built from several smaller bricks.

Why does this matter? Cost, speed and the context limit are all measured in tokens. It explains odd behaviour (letter counting, some languages costing more). A few key words. Token: A chunk of text from the model's vocabulary. Tokenizer: The tool that splits text into tokens and I Ds. Vocabulary: The fixed list of all tokens a model knows. Context window: Max tokens per request (input plus output).
Text leads to Tokens leads to I Ds. An L L M never sees letters or words. A tokenizer first chops the text into pieces called tokens.
Common words stay whole ( love ). Rarer words split into frequent sub-pieces: un plus believ plus able. The leading space is part of the token.
Each token maps to an integer I D in a fixed vocabulary (roughly 32k–200k entries). These integers are all the model ever sees.
Each I D picks a row from the embedding matrix, giving a vector of numbers the transformer can do math on.
Rule of thumb for English: 1 token about 4 characters about ¾ of a word, so 1,000 tokens is about 750 words. Code and non-English text usually take more tokens per word.
Context window & cost. Everything you send is tokens: system prompt, chat history, retrieved chunks and the question.
All of it must fit in the context window, the maximum number of tokens per request (input plus output).
Prefill: the model reads all input tokens in parallel. This sets the time to first token.
Decode: output is generated one token at a time. That's why streaming works, and why long answers take longer.
If history grows past the window you must truncate, summarize or retrieve. Otherwise the call fails or old context gets dropped.
Cost equals input tokens times input price plus output tokens times output price. Output tokens usually cost several times more, so keep answers tight.

What a token is. A token is a chunk of text from the model's fixed vocabulary: a whole word, part of a word, a space plus a word, punctuation or bytes. The model predicts the next token, never the next word.

How B P E (Byte-Pair Encoding) builds the vocabulary. Start with single bytes or characters as the vocabulary. Count every adjacent pair in a huge corpus and merge the most frequent pair into a new token (for example t plus h leads to th ). Repeat until the vocabulary reaches its target size. Result: common words become one token, rare words become several, and nothing is ever "unknown".

Why interviewers care. Cost & latency scale with tokens, especially output tokens. Context limits are measured in tokens, which drives chunk size in rag and history trimming. Quirks: letter counting ("how many r's in strawberry") and arithmetic are hard because the model sees chunks, not characters. Languages: Hindi, Tamil and many other languages can take 2–4 times more tokens than English for the same meaning, so they cost more and fill the window faster.

Special tokens & chat templates. Models use reserved tokens to mark structure: beginning and end of text, and role markers for system / user / assistant. The chat A P I wraps your messages in this template for you. Generation stops at an end-of-sequence (E O S) token or at max tokens.

Analogy. Think L E G O: the tokenizer has a fixed box of bricks. Common shapes come pre-built ("the", " love"); unusual shapes get built from smaller bricks. The model only ever plays with brick numbers.

Common mistakes. Assuming word count equals token count. Comparing token counts across vendors. Each model family has its own tokenizer, so the same text gives different counts. Forgetting that output tokens count against the context window too.

Say it in the interview. "L L Ms operate on subword tokens produced by a tokenizer like B P E. Each token maps to an I D, then to an embedding vector. Tokens drive cost, latency and context limits. In rag that's why I size chunks in tokens and budget the window: system prompt, retrieved context, history, and headroom for the answer.".

Tokenization strategies. Word-level: whole words, huge (100k+), short sequences, unknown words (O O V), huge vocab. Character-level: single chars, tiny (~100s), no O O V, very long sequences, slow. Subword (B P E / WordPiece / SentencePiece): frequent chunks, 32k–200k, no O O V, good balance, odd splits, language bias.

A likely interview question: What is a token and why does it matter? A strong answer: A subword unit from the tokenizer's vocabulary. It matters because cost, latency and context limits are all measured in tokens.
That's it for Tokens & Tokenization. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
